title: County (United States)
description: Subdivision used by most states in the United States
wiki_lead:
In the United States, a county or county equivalent is an administrative subdivision of a state or territory, typically with defined geographic boundaries and some level of governmental authority. The term "county" is used in 47 states, while Louisiana, Alaska, and Connecticut have functionally "county equivalent" subdivisions called parishes, boroughs, and councils of governments or planning regions, respectively. County equivalents also include consolidated city-counties, in which a municipality has been consolidated with its county government, and independent cities, in which a municipality has been legally separated from counties altogether. The District of Columbia is considered a single county equivalent for administrative purposes. In addition, the United States Census Bureau further divides Alaska's Unorganized Borough into 11 census areas that are statistically equivalent to counties.
Counties and other local governments exist as a matter of U.S. state law, so the specific governmental powers of counties may vary widely between the states, with many providing some level of services to municipalities, civil townships, and unincorporated areas. Certain municipalities are in multiple counties. Counties in Hawaii handle almost all services since there is no formal level of government (municipality, public education, or otherwise) in that state that exists below that of the county. Conversely, counties in Rhode Island, Connecticut's historical counties, eight of Massachusetts's 14 counties, and Alaska's Unorganized Borough and its 11 census areas have no government power, existing only as geographic distinctions.
Territories of the United States do not have counties; instead, the United States Census Bureau also divides them into county equivalents. The U.S. Census Bureau counts American Samoa's districts and atolls as county equivalents. American Samoa locally has places called "counties", but these entities are considered to be "minor civil divisions" (not true counties) by the U.S. Census Bureau.
The number of counties per state ranges from the three counties of Delaware to the 254 counties of Texas. County populations also vary widely; in 2017, according to the Census Bureau, more than half the U.S. population was concentrated in just 143 of the more than 3,000 counties, or just 4.6% of all counties. As of 2017, the five most populous counties, ordered from most to least, were Los Angeles County, California; Cook County, Illinois; Harris County, Texas; Maricopa County, Arizona; and San Diego County, California.
As of 2022, there are 3,144 counties and county equivalents in the 50 states and the District of Columbia. If the 100 county equivalents in the U.S. territories are counted, then the total is 3,244 counties and county equivalents in the United States.

grok_lead: In the United States, a county is the primary legal subdivision of most states, functioning as a unit of local government with responsibilities that typically include recording deeds, administering probate courts, conducting elections, providing for public safety, and maintaining roads. As of 2022, there are 3,143 counties and county-equivalent entities across the nation, encompassing divisions in 48 states, parishes in Louisiana, organized and unorganized boroughs in Alaska, and the District of Columbia. These entities originated as extensions of state authority but have evolved into key providers of mandated services such as human services, criminal justice, public welfare, and infrastructure, often operating under varying degrees of home rule granted by state legislatures. Counties play a central role in the federal system by decentralizing governance, enabling localized administration of laws and collection of property taxes that fund essential operations, though their exact powers differ significantly by state.
